---
title: "Research"
---

My research is centred on molecular simulation methods for chemically complex soft-matter systems.

The systems I study are often heterogeneous, slowly evolving and organized over multiple length scales. They include polymers, surfactants, membranes, nanocomposites, grafted interfaces, brushes and nanoplastics.

The common methodological question is how to connect molecular identity with collective organization.

## Coarse-grained molecular models

Coarse-grained models make it possible to study molecular systems beyond the length and time scales accessible to fully atomistic simulations.

In my work, coarse-graining has not been only a way to reduce computational cost. It has been a way to ask how much molecular information is needed to describe structure, organization and material behaviour.

## Reverse mapping

Reverse mapping connects simplified molecular representations back to more detailed atomistic structures.

This has been an important part of my work because it preserves a link between efficient coarse-grained simulations and chemically realistic molecular models.

## Hybrid particle--field molecular dynamics

Hybrid particle--field molecular dynamics combines molecular particles with density fields.

Particles preserve molecular architecture, connectivity and chemical identity. Density fields describe collective non-bonded interactions and mesoscale organization.

This approach is especially useful for dense and complex soft-matter systems, where many-body organization is central.

## Chemically complex soft matter

I have applied and extended these methods to a range of soft-matter systems, including:

- polymer melts and polymer nanocomposites;
- surfactants and amphiphilic assemblies;
- biomembranes and lipid systems;
- grafted polymers and brushes;
- carbon black--polymer interfaces;
- micro- and nanoplastics.

These systems are diverse, but they share a common feature: their behaviour depends on both molecular chemistry and collective organization.

## Density-based descriptions

A recurring theme in my current work is the role of density-based descriptions in molecular simulation.

Density fields can provide a language for composition, morphology, interfaces and mesoscale structure. The challenge is to keep this language connected to chemistry, rather than turning it into a generic continuum description.
